entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Fakhr-un-Nisa Shuhdah Umm Muhammad al-Baghdadiyyah (died 1112 CE), often known simply as Shuhdah al-Baghdadiyyah, was a preeminent Kurdish scholar, muhaddithah (female hadith scholar), and calligrapher whose intellectual prowess and teaching authority left an indelible mark on Islamic scholarship in 11th and 12th-century Baghdad. Revered as 'the calligrapher' and 'the pride of womanhood,' her distinction lay in her exceptionally high isnad (chain of transmission for hadith), connecting her directly to some of the most esteemed early Islamic scholars. Her life and work exemplify the significant, though often underappreciated, roles women played in transmitting religious knowledge during the Classical Islamic Golden Age, particularly within the Abbasid Caliphate's cultural heartland.

Shuhdah's early education in Baghdad, a vibrant center of learning, was meticulously overseen by her father, Abu Nasr Ahmad ibn al-Faraj al-Ibari, himself a distinguished scholar. She received ijaza (authorization to transmit knowledge) from numerous prominent male and female scholars, including Abu Abdullah al-Barani and Abu al-Khattab Nasr ibn Ahmad al-Batir, allowing her to teach a vast corpus of hadith, fiqh (Islamic jurisprudence), and Arabic linguistics. Her academic rigor extended to calligraphy, a highly respected art form, where her mastery earned her the appellation 'the calligrapher.' She maintained a large madrasa (school) in Baghdad, attracting students from across the Islamic world, where she lectured well into her later years.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Fakhr-un-Nisa was a pivotal figure in the transmission of Islamic knowledge, recognized for her exceptionally high isnad and her role in educating hundreds of students across the Islamic world. Her life demonstrates the significant, though often overlooked, contributions of women to religious scholarship during the Abbasid era, influencing the continuity of prophetic traditions.
